Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

mara had told me the day before that if the rain began before noon we should move the spinach and mint into the back crate under the table and leave the strawberry display at the front only if the arcade steward confirmed the awning was secure at eight twenty the steward checked the ties and said they were holding but asked us to keep the folded side panel ready because the wind was expected to come through the north passage when a shower started around eleven we moved the spinach and mint as planned and kept the strawberries at the front the awning did not flap loose and the side panel stayed folded the condition about checking with the steward mattered because we would otherwise have moved the whole display away from the aisle

The stall is on the east side of the covered arcade beside the blue post, not the entrance facing the bus stop. I got there at 6:40 because the driver had asked us to leave room for his hand trolley between the flower stand and our table. The forecast said showers after lunch, and the pavement was already damp, but there was no rain while we unloaded. Mara, our stall lead, had the key to the padlock, and I had the paper order and a pencil. The driver was Leon from Bell Orchard, and he said the van had left the farm at 5:20 after the cold-room check.

We received fourteen wooden crates of strawberries, six shallow trays of rhubarb, two sacks of spinach, and a small box of mint. The strawberry crates were marked with the picking date, and the rhubarb trays had blue tape around the corners. One crate had a split slat, but the fruit inside looked intact. I counted the crates twice because the first count came to thirteen—no, fourteen—and Mara counted them again with me. The invoice listed the same quantities except it called the mint a mixed herb box. Leon said that was how their printer described it, and I wrote “mint” on our stall copy. The order total was two hundred and eighty-six pounds, including the twelve-pound delivery fee, which we had agreed by email on Monday.

While we were checking the fruit, Mara asked whether the strawberries had stayed in the chilled part of the van. Leon said yes; the temperature display had read four degrees when they left and five degrees when he opened the back doors here at the arcade. I asked if the display reading was written on his sheet. He said, “It is on the route copy in the cab.” He went back to get it, and the route copy showed four degrees at departure and five degrees at arrival. It did not show a reading for the drive itself. Mara said, “Right, that answers the question for the arrival time,” and then she wrote both numbers on the receiving sheet. She did not say that we had checked the temperature throughout the trip.

1. Mara checked the strawberries for soft patches and set the split crate on the lower shelf so it would not be lifted again.
2. I weighed the rhubarb trays and found that one was short by about three hundred grams compared with the label. Mara said we should note the weight and email the orchard before deciding whether it affected the invoice.
3. We checked the spinach sacks and found one damp patch on the outside, but the leaves in that sack were dry.
4. I put the mint box in the lidded tub away from the strawberries because the mint smell was strong enough to carry across the table.
5. Leon took away the empty hand trolley and left the wooden crates stacked behind the stall.

At 7:10, we put the price cards out but did not start selling the strawberries until Mara had taken a photograph of the split crate and the short rhubarb tray. She sent the pictures to our shared account and wrote that the strawberry fruit appeared intact and that one rhubarb tray seemed underweight. Leon said, “Send me the photo too, and I will attach it to the route record.” I sent it to the number on his delivery slip. He replied that he had received it and would pass it to the orchard office. He did not offer a replacement or say that the invoice would change, and we did not ask him to decide either point at the stall.

Mara had told me the day before that if the rain began before noon, we should move the spinach and mint into the back crate under the table and leave the strawberry display at the front only if the arcade steward confirmed the awning was secure. At 8:20, the steward checked the ties and said they were holding, but asked us to keep the folded side panel ready because the wind was expected to come through the north passage. When a shower started around eleven, we moved the spinach and mint as planned and kept the strawberries at the front. The awning did not flap loose, and the side panel stayed folded. The condition about checking with the steward mattered because we would otherwise have moved the whole display away from the aisle.

By midday, we had sold three punnets of strawberries and one bundle of rhubarb, and there were no complaints from customers about the fruit. Mara wrote those sales on the chalkboard tally rather than in the delivery record. The remaining strawberries stayed in the shaded front display, and we kept the damp spinach sack separate so its outer surface would not touch the other produce. At 1:15, the rain eased, and the steward said we could put the side panel away. I asked Mara whether she wanted me to update the shared account with that information, and she said not yet because the delivery photos and the weather note were enough for now. She asked me to keep the paper order beside the receiving sheet until she had compared the invoice with the orchard reply.

When I left at 2:30, the short rhubarb tray was still listed as a question on the receiving sheet, and the invoice total remained two hundred and eighty-six pounds. The orchard office had not replied yet. Mara had the delivery slip and the route copy, and I put the stall copy in the blue folder in the drawer. The next market delivery was due on Saturday at 6:30, but we had not changed that booking. We had agreed that if the orchard replied before then, Mara would review the weight and the invoice with me; otherwise, we would keep the note open and ask them about it when the next driver arrived."}]
